results.title: Uncertainty quantification // van der Schaar Lab
results.content: The successful application of machine learning models to real-world prediction problems requires us to be able to limit and quantify the uncertainty in model predictions by providing valid and accurate prediction intervals. While machine learning models may achieve high predictive accuracy across a broad spectrum of tasks, rigorously quantifying their predictive uncertainty remains challenging. Bayesian neural networks, which are frequently used in methods for uncertainty quantification, tend to exhibit over-confidence in predictions made on target data whose feature distribution differs from the training data; furthermore, they do not provide frequentist coverage guarantees, cannot be applied post-hoc, and their approximate posterior inference undermines discriminative accuracy. As detailed below, our methods (most of which have been introduced in papers published in top-tier AI and machine learning conferences) address the shortcomings of existing approaches to uncertainty quantification, and significantly outperform benchmark methods. While existing variants of BNNs based on Monte Carlo dropout produce reliable (albeit approximate) uncertainty estimates over in-distribution data, they tend to exhibit over-confidence in predictions made on target data whose feature distribution differs from the training data, i.e., the covariate shift setup. Existing methods for uncertainty quantification are based predominantly on Bayesian neural networks; these may fall short of (1) and (2) — i.e., Bayesian credible intervals do not guarantee frequentist coverage, and approximate posterior inference undermines discriminative accuracy. Existing methods for uncertainty quantification in RNN-based time-series forecasts are limited as they may require significant alterations to the underlying architecture, may be computationally complex, may be difficult to calibrate, may incur high sample complexity, and may not provide theoretical validity guarantees for the issued uncertainty intervals. Successful application of machine learning models to real-world prediction problems, e.g. financial forecasting and personalized medicine, has proved to be challenging, because such settings require limiting and quantifying the uncertainty in the model predictions, i.e. providing valid and accurate prediction intervals. Among the various tools available, **credible intervals** provide a probabilistic interpretation that is especially useful when making decisions based on uncertain evidence. This guide offers a practical, hands-on tutorial for computing, visualizing, and interpreting Bayesian credible intervals. ### Overview of Credible Intervals In Bayesian inference, a credible interval is the range of parameter values within which a given proportion of the posterior probability distribution lies. Formally, if we denote the parameter of interest by θ\theta θ, a 95% credible interval [a,b][a, b][a,b] is constructed such that: P(a≤θ≤b∣data)=0.95 P(a \leq \theta \leq b | \text{data}) = 0.95 P(a≤θ≤b∣data)=0.95 Unlike frequentist confidence intervals, these intervals allow us to directly state the probability of the parameter lying within a certain range given our preceding assumptions and observed data. ### Benefits in Practice Key advantages of Bayesian credible intervals include: * **Direct probabilistic interpretation**: They answer questions such as “What is the probability that the parameter lies in this range?” without resorting to long-run frequency interpretations. * **Adaptability in complex models**: When analytic solutions are intractable, simulation-based methods can approximate credible intervals efficiently. A clear setup of the Bayesian model is essential to understanding and computing credible intervals. When conditions permit, analytical or closed-form solutions for the posterior distribution can be derived, leading to easier computation of credible intervals. These diagnostics help identify whether the chain has reached its stationary distribution and whether the credible intervals computed from the samples are representative of the posterior. Once credible intervals have been computed and visualized, interpreting these intervals properly is crucial for making informed decisions. * **Posterior Analysis**: The computed posterior reveals a 95% credible interval for the reduction effect that does not include zero. * Computing credible intervals both analytically and through simulation methods like MCMC. results.title: Mastering Bayesian Credible Regions
results.content: This article delves into the theoretical foundations, computational methods, and practical applications of credible regions in Bayesian analysis. In Bayesian analysis, a **credible region** is defined as a subset of the parameter space for which the true parameter value lies with a specified posterior probability. A credible region, therefore, is directly derived from this posterior and can be expressed as: $$ \int\_{C} p(\theta \mid \mathbf{X}) , d\theta = 1 - \alpha, $$ where $C$ is the credible region, typically chosen such that \_USD\_1 - \alpha$ (e.g., \_USD\_0.95$ for a 95% credible region) of the posterior mass is contained within $C$. * **Credible Interval (Bayesian):** A 95% credible interval means that there is a 95% probability that the true parameter value falls inside the interval, based on the posterior distribution. The elegance of Bayes’ theorem lies in its ability to combine prior information with observed data to produce the posterior, which is used for constructing credible regions. This approach involves discretely approximating the integral that defines the posterior and then computing credible regions from the resulting numerical distribution. Several real-world case studies highlight the utility of credible regions in Bayesian data analysis:. Bayesian credible regions provide a robust framework for uncertainty quantification that aligns naturally with the Bayesian paradigm of probability. By defining intervals based on the posterior distribution, credible regions offer a clear and direct interpretation of uncertainty that is particularly useful in decision-making contexts. * Practical applications across diverse fields, illustrating how credible regions inform parameter estimation in both simple and complex models. Embracing credible regions as part of your Bayesian toolkit not only enhances the clarity of your uncertainty quantification but also builds a strong foundation for more sophisticated statistical modeling. By integrating rigorous mathematical theory with practical computational techniques and real-world applications, this guide aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to credible regions in Bayesian analysis.
